papers.title: Four-dimensional QCD equation of state with a critical surface from contours of constant entropy density
papers.summary: We present a new lattice-QCD-based equation of state in the four-dimensional space of $(T,μ_B,μ_Q,μ_S)$ which features a critical surface. This is obtained by generalizing the expansion of constant entropy density contours across the multiple conserved charges of QCD. Since this expansion permits the presence of a first-order phase transition, this is the first lattice QCD based equation of state in four dimensions with a critical surface. We parametrize the chemical potential space using spherical coordinates $(μ,θ,\varphi)$, reducing the problem to a one-dimensional extrapolation in $(T,μ)$ at fixed angles that, together, span the full 4D space. By integrating the extrapolated entropy density, we reconstruct the pressure, from which we obtain the conserved charge densities, their susceptibilities and the speed of sound. Our results agree quantitatively with other lattice QCD constructions at low chemical potentials in the crossover region, and predict the emergence of a first-order phase transition at higher chemical potentials. We study equation of state properties in detail under heavy-ion collision (HIC) conditions for the strangeness and electric charge densities ($n_S=0,~n_Q=0.4n_B$), where we find the CP location at $(T_c,μ_{B,c},μ_{Q,c},μ_{S,c})=(115\pm7,646\pm72,-12\pm3,117\pm16)$ MeV. In particular, we find a strong non-monotonic dependence of baryon number susceptibilities along the chemical freeze-out line at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} \lesssim 7.7$ GeV. Finally, we outline further applications of the 4D equation of state, including charge-neutral matter relevant to neutron stars and large isospin density relevant to cosmic trajectories in the early Universe.

papers.title: EEG-Based Prediction of Music Enjoyment Using Deep Learning with Explainable Temporal Analysis
papers.summary: Understanding why listeners enjoy music is difficult because the experience is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive way to study neural responses during listening, yet earlier work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. We formulate enjoyment prediction as a regression problem on the public MUSIN-G dataset, which contains 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners together with song-level enjoyment ratings. Six deep learning models were compared under a participant-wise protocol, in which 15 listeners were used for training and validation and 5 were held out for testing. DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM and GNN-CNN reached the lowest mean absolute error (0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale), while the temporal convolutional network (TCN) had the highest Pearson correlation with the ratings (r = 0.21). Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations, averaged over all held-out windows, identify the time segments within each two-second window that most influence the TCN predictions. The study provides a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression and shows how explainability analysis complements standard metrics.

papers.title: Optimal Strategies for Gravitational-Wave Memory Detection with Noise Marginalization in Pulsar Timing Arrays
papers.summary: Current pulsar timing arrays could detect gravitational wave memory, which would provide a unique test of general relativity. In order to optimize our searches for gravitational wave memory in pulsar timing arrays, we integrate the optimal frequentist statistics for GW memory into the \texttt{enterprise} code suite. We additionally test a noise marginalized version of this statistic, and compare it's effectiveness to the simpler maximum posterior method. We perform these tests on simulated pulsar timing array with red and white noise content, as well as the NANOGrav $15$-year data set. We find no significant variations in our detection statistics between the noise-marginalized and the maximum-posterior methods for the simulated datasets, and only small variations in the NANOGrav $15$-year comparisons. We conclude that for realistic PTAs the noise-marginalization method could be useful for assigning a false alarm probability to Bayesian results, though the maximum posterior method is sufficient for identifying potentially detectable signals.
papers.comment: 8 page paper on methods development for gravitational wave memory searches in pulsar timing arrays, tested with both simulated and real datasets

papers.title: All Order Gravitational Wave Tails for Subleading Post-Newtonian Expansion
papers.summary: The low-frequency gravitational waveform emitted in a classical scattering process contains an infinite tower of late- and early-time tail terms of the form $u^{-r}(\ln|u|)^{r-1}$, $r \geq 1$. In the Newtonian limit, the coefficients of this entire tower have recently been shown to be universal, i.e. fixed by the asymptotic data of the scattering objects alone. At the retained order in the velocity expansion, these leading-logarithmic tails are determined to all orders in Newton's constant $G$. We extend this result to the first subleading order in the post-Newtonian expansion of the asymptotic states. We consider scattering of an arbitrary number of incoming and outgoing nonrelativistic objects interacting only through gravity at long range, and we derive the complete tower of tail terms at this order. The correction arises from the first subleading term in the retardation expansion and is determined by the asymptotic Newtonian trajectories of the massive particles. Its coefficients are again determined entirely by the asymptotic trajectories and are independent of the details of the interaction. For $2\to2$ scattering, the leading-logarithmic series can be summed in closed form. Our results agree with a relativistic conjecture proposed in earlier work arXiv:2610.07134.

papers.title: Semantic Alignment of EEG and Text: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Decoding Imagined Speech
papers.summary: Imagined speech decoding from EEG offers a promising route toward naturalistic brain-computer interfaces. Traditional closed-set classifiers treat semantic categories as independent labels and do not explicitly exploit relationships among linguistic intents, limiting output flexibility. We adapt a multimodal contrastive learning framework to imagined speech, aligning EEG trials with language representations in the embedding space of a frozen pretrained text encoder. An EEG encoder is trained with a composite objective combining semantically reweighted EEG-sentence alignment and text-prototype-based class discrimination, encouraging semantic structure while preserving separability among 39 intent categories. We evaluate the approach on the Chisco imagined speech dataset across five subjects, reporting Top-k accuracy, macro-F1, and balanced pairwise matching accuracy (2v2). We also investigate maximum EEG-text cosine similarity (MaxCosine) as an intrinsic indicator of decoding reliability and probe semantic structure beyond category labels using five evaluation-time semantic axes and a qualitative Semantic Gallery Probe (SGP) with previously unseen candidate sentences. The contrastive framework achieved decoding performance comparable to a task-optimized closed-set classifier while mapping EEG into a frozen language embedding space. MaxCosine identified subsets of held-out trials with higher Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy across subjects. Evaluation-time semantic axes showed mean agreement above the 50% chance reference across all five dimensions, and the SGP qualitatively illustrated direct comparison with unseen candidate sentences. Together, these findings suggest that EEG-language alignment can retain comparable fixed-intent decoding while supporting similarity-based retrieval, intrinsic reliability ranking, and evaluation of broader semantic structure.

papers.title: Nonlocal Gravity, Restricted CPL Dynamics and DESI Constraints
papers.summary: Nonlocal modifications of gravity provide a theoretically motivated framework in which cosmic acceleration can emerge dynamically without introducing a fundamental cosmological constant. We revisit the cosmological predictions of the Maggiore--Mancarella nonlocal $R\,\Box^{-2}R$ model, with particular emphasis on its background dynamics and observational viability in light of recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation measurements. A key feature of the theory is its predictive character: for fixed standard cosmological parameters, each value of the nonlocal parameter determines a specific effective pair $(w_0,w_a)$, so that the model traces a restricted trajectory in the Chevallier--Polarski--Linder plane rather than spanning the full phenomenological parameter space. We construct this mapping explicitly and confront the model with observations by implementing its cosmological dynamics in a Boltzmann solver and performing a Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis using Cosmic Microwave Background, supernova, and DESI BAO data. We find that current datasets constrain the nonlocal parameter close to the $Λ$CDM limit, with no statistically significant preference for nonlocal deviations.

papers.title: Towards ultrarelativistic scattering near the light ring: asymptotic divergence of gravitational-wave fluxes
papers.summary: Near the threshold between scattering and capture by a Schwarzschild black hole, a particle spends a long time close to an unstable circular orbit, which in the ultrarelativistic limit approaches the light ring. Here we study the behavior of the gravitational wave fluxes emitted by such an ultrarelativistic particle at first order in the mass ratio. The fluxes radiated to infinity and absorbed by the horizon diverge as the inverse distance from the light ring multiplied by its logarithm. Using the Wentzel, Kramers, and Brillouin (WKB) approximation to solve the Regge-Wheeler equation and treating the infinite harmonic sum analytically, we derive an exact expression for the coefficient of this logarithmic enhancement and show that it is identical for both fluxes. We then estimate the coefficients of the subleading pole contributions by combining numerical calculations at low multipoles with the exact asymptotics at large multipoles. We further conjecture an extension to equatorial circular orbits in Kerr. Interestingly, our results also inform the analytical structure of the energy and angular momentum losses of ultrarelativistic scattering orbits near the light ring. More broadly, our work illustrates how WKB methods can provide the asymptotic behavior of self-force observables in regimes where numerical mode sums become increasingly challenging.

papers.title: Quantum critical collapse in the large $D$ limit
papers.summary: In analytically tractable models of Einstein-scalar critical collapse, it has been shown that the quantum self-energy of the collapsing matter in the dominant $s$-wave sector grows with Lyapunov exponent $D-2$, eventually competing with the classical instability that controls black hole formation. This competition shifts the naked singularity threshold and produces a finite mass gap within semiclassical control, yet that control may appear threatened as the spacetime dimension $D\to\infty$. We study this quantum growing mode in both continuously (CSS) and discretely (DSS) self-similar critical spacetimes at large $D$ and establish that the universal Lyapunov exponent survives both forms of self-similarity. In CSS, the classical approach to a naked singularity is interrupted by the appearance of trapped surfaces. At large $D$, the horizon tracing reduces to a Bessel problem, yielding a quantum wall whose radius obeys $r_h\propto(D-2)^{-2}$. This radius can remain above the Planck scale at finite $D$, although maintaining this hierarchy becomes increasingly demanding as $D$ grows. In DSS, the same growth is modulated by echoing and can retain memory of previous echoes. The simplest anomaly-induced action exhibits accumulating memory but is singular at the spherical center. We construct a covariant one-loop action whose stress tensor remains smooth throughout the DSS domain and organize it into an echo-periodic structure without memory. This suggests that the smooth vacuum polarization of the genuine four-dimensional DSS Choptuik spacetime may similarly be governed by its exact echoing symmetry.

papers.title: Player-1: Learning to Play from Synthetic Experience
papers.summary: Computer-use agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions. However, games, with their visually rich worlds and diverse mechanics, remain challenging and offer a demanding next step toward general digital control. Current game-agent learning pipelines often rely on large-scale demonstrations with limited coverage of dynamic game states, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain. We introduce Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience. We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions. For supervised initialization, we fine-tune computer-use models on 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories that pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning. We construct Player-1-Gym, sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around control demands shared across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with PPO. The resulting Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B improve MineDojo-300 success over their SFT policies by 27.8 and 17.7 percentage points, respectively. Player-1-9B reaches 38.33% success compared with 12.63% for the strongest evaluated baseline, with further gains over SFT on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld. Further analyses show that broader synthetic environment coverage improves transfer, while the use of composite actions that combine multiple keyboard and mouse inputs increases during RL. We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience substantially improves game control beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.
papers.comment: Project Page: https://player-1-project.github.io/ and code: https://github.com/TencentARC/Player-1

papers.title: Speculative Sampling in Interactive Video Generation
papers.summary: Interactive video generation commonly relies on small bidirectional chunks to reduce response latency. Yet our preliminary experiments show that larger chunks improve video quality and better utilize GPU parallelism, allowing more latents to be sampled with only a modest increase in sampling time. Motivated by these observations, we propose Speculative Sampling, a strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window by appending noise latents as padding and caches the resulting predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged. Predictions are delivered incrementally, while the uncommitted future remains replaceable. Our latency analysis shows that this removes the waiting-time lower bound imposed by chunk boundaries, shifting the optimization focus from reducing chunk size to accelerating per-chunk sampling. Bidirectional window size thus becomes a decision variable for jointly optimizing visual quality and sampling time, rather than a necessary constraint on low-latency interaction. This opens a path to serving large bidirectional models in interactive streaming systems without complex streaming post-training.

papers.title: Prospects for modelling odd and odd-odd nuclei using energy density functionals
papers.summary: About half of particle-bound nuclei have an odd number of nucleons. About one quarter more are odd-odd, meaning they have an odd number of neutrons and an odd number of protons. In this context, it is about time to shift the 70-odd-year focus of theories using nuclear energy density functionals (EDFs) away from the remaining one-quarter of even-even nuclei. This White Paper aims to present open, unresolved problems and promising research directions in nuclear EDFs that were discussed during the 2024 ESNT workshop in Saclay, France, on ``The microscopic modelling of odd-mass and odd-odd nuclei''.
papers.comment: White Paper, 80 LaTeX pages, 21 figures, comments welcome

papers.title: Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans (ImpactBench): an expert-guided, open platform for the holistic evaluation of AI impact on humans
papers.summary: The present work is concerned with how to measure, at scale, the multi-dimensional impact of generative AI models on the individuals who use them. In service of this goal, we introduce the Open Benchmark of AI Impact on Humans, or ImpactBench. Our iterable and expert-guided platform evaluates whether model behaviors support or undermine an individual's wellbeing across psychological, physical, and social domains. ImpactBench translates constructs from domain experts and existing benchmarks into metrics that are grounded in actual model behavior. Success on these metrics occurs either when a model promotes expert-defined desirable behaviors or avoids identified harms. Models are evaluated against these metrics in simulated multi-turn conversations using matched teen and adult scenarios. The conversations are then scored by an LLM judge and verified through reliability audits and human expert review. The current suite delivers 809 metrics drawn from 26 benchmarks. We evaluated ten frontier LLMs against these metrics across 48,540 conversations. Our results indicate that models promoted desirable behaviors in 68.7% of evaluations, but avoided harms in only 53.1%. Majority expert ratings agreed with the automated judge in 83.3% of reviewed cases (Cohen's Kappa = 0.667). Results are released through a public platform that keep aggregate scores traceable to the underlying metrics and transcripts. ImpactBench is intended as evolving infrastructure for independent, transparent evaluation of generative AI's multi-dimensional impact on humans.
authors: Andre Luiz Freire de Carvalho Kato

papers.title: Evolution of multihadron fragmentation functions with nonperturbative behavior
papers.summary: QCD calculations that use multihadron fragmentation functions usually involve multiple invariant mass scales simultaneously, with only one being the hard scale associated with an overall hard process. The other scales are associated with relative internal motion intrinsic to the fragmenting parton and the multihadron system. Nonperturbative contributions to this later type of dependence attract interest for their association with intrinsic partonic structures, but care is needed in disentangling the truly nonperturbative effects from perturbative behavior and relating the former to universal nonperturbative matrix elements. To this end, we show how to evolve collinear multihadron fragmentation functions in a way that accounts for the simultaneous presence of these extra scales. The general multihadron fragmentation functions evolve in the same way as ordinary single hadron fragmentation functions, with the dependence on the extra scales separated out. We use this to unify treatments of perturbative and nonperturbative effects in multihadron systems in a way that optimizes for interpretations focused on partonic structure.

papers.title: Revealing Structured Heterogeneity
papers.summary: In this paper, we study models of restricted heterogeneity. While the random utility model allows for arbitrary heterogeneity among rational types, we consider the case when an analyst ex-ante restricts the set of rational types to some smaller set of allowable types. We study the behavioral content, the model fit, and the identification properties of restrictions of this form. We find that all three of these can be connected through a common value function that is constructed from observable data. Consistency with a model of restricted heterogeneity is characterized by this value function achieving a value of one, while model fit is given by a value that is potentially less than one. The partially identified set for a given model of restricted heterogeneity is characterized by way of the subdifferential of this value function.

papers.title: Fast Monte Carlo calculation of multiple scattering in resonant neutron capture
papers.summary: A fast Monte Carlo code has been developed to calculate multiple neutron scattering in a sample. Good agreement with an independent Monte Carlo calculation using SAMMY is obtained for neutron capture in $^{197}$Au over the energy range 50--300 eV. For capture following two or more scattering events, a difference is found between the direct Monte Carlo calculation and the analytical approximation in SAMMY. The computational speed allows the scattering correction to be recalculated whenever trial resonance parameters are changed during parameter estimation. The computational core is implemented in C++, while data preparation, calculation control and analysis are performed in Python. Model studies examine how Monte Carlo statistics affect the accuracy with which neutron and radiative resonance widths are recovered.

papers.title: Universal enhancement of the pairing gap in a dilute Fermi superfluid
papers.summary: At zero temperature, a dilute Fermi gas with an attractive contact interaction forms a superfluid with gapped fermionic excitations. We show that the gap at weak coupling can be organized as a trans-series expansion in the interaction strength and the asymptotic Gor'kov-Melik-Barkhudarov gap. Low-energy virtual quasiparticles generate corrections that are linear in the gap with a leading coefficient nearly 25$\times$ larger than the other known coefficients. This substantially increases the gap at intermediate densities, highlighting that systematic corrections are crucial for quantitative predictions.

papers.title: Regime Detection in Latent Factor Models -- A Bayesian Decision-Theoretic Approach
papers.summary: Regime-switching multi-factor models are widely used in quantitative finance, but filtering does not by itself determine when an agent should act on inferred regime changes. We formulate online regime detection with latent factors and hidden regimes as a Bayesian decision problem balancing false alarms, detection delay, and misclassification. Since posterior regime probabilities are generally non-Markovian, the problem is represented as a measure-valued optimal stopping problem and approximated using particle filtering with Monte Carlo dynamic programming. A single-change-point Heston model provides a benchmark. With observed variance, the problem reduces to a two-dimensional Markov free-boundary problem, while under latent variance decisions are based on the filtered posterior measure. Numerical experiments in Heston and regime-switching Vasicek models show that the latent-information procedure can outperform feasible plug-in rules.

papers.title: Excited-State Effects in Nucleon Sigma Terms from a Variational Analysis
papers.summary: We investigate excited-state effects in nucleon sigma-terms in lattice QCD using twisted-mass clover-improved fermion ensembles. We study correlation functions with nucleon and multihadron nucleon-$σ$-meson interpolating operators. The analysis is performed using three gauge ensembles, including one ensemble simulated with two degenerate light, a strange, and a charm quark with quark masses tuned to approximately their physical value. We solve the generalized eigenvalue problem that arises from the matrix of correlators and show that the three-point function for the light sigma-term obtained using the optimal linear combination of interpolating operators has substantially reduced time dependence without loss of statistical precision. We apply Laplace filtering and investigate residual excited-state contributions in the extraction of $σ_{πN}$. Using the same optimal linear combination of correlators as for $σ_{πN}$ for the strange sigma-term we also observe suppressed excited state contributions over an extended range of source--sink time separations. For the charm sigma-term, we observe negligible time dependence within the large statistical uncertainties, and these improvements show no significant effect.

papers.title: Predicting Unseen Scientific Interactions: Conditional Flow Models Hallucinate Non-Additive Effects
papers.summary: Conditional generative models are increasingly used for scientific prediction beyond the direct training support. Yet scientific questions often concern whether one intervention changes the effect of another. Such interactions can be of primary interest while explaining little of the total variation, allowing models to appear accurate overall without recovering the relevant scientific effect. It remains unclear how these models learn interactions and when these successfully extrapolate to unseen conditions. We therefore study interaction recovery in flow-matching models using a physiological time-series simulator, drug dose-response data, combinatorial cell perturbations, and molecular conformer generations, where we separate recovery from hallucinated interaction structure. In the controlled setting, individual effects are learned much earlier than interactions and models hallucinate interactions where none exist. Across settings, we find qualitatively different generalization problems, with successful prediction depending on whether condition structure continues from observed to held-out targets. When it does, interactions are recoverable. If not, models can generate plausible responses while missing the interaction. We furthermore find that hallucinations increase as targets become less identifiable, and that successful interaction recovery in output space can fail under nonlinear readouts. Finally, we show that aggregate fidelity metrics can conceal whether models learn and extrapolate interactions.
papers.comment: Accepted as an oral at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: AI Data Readiness for Scientific Discovery (AIDaR). Code: https://github.com/SamGijsen/interaction-flows

papers.title: From Semantic Editing Intentions to Persistent Parametric Controls for AI-Assisted Image Editing
papers.summary: AI-powered image editing increasingly allows users to express high-level editing intentions, yet how these intentions are translated into concrete editing actions often remains difficult to understand. We present Atelier, a semantic image editing tool that uses image semantics and user intent to determine which editing controls to surface and how to initialize them. Guided by a formative study with eight image-editing practitioners, Atelier composes context-specific, directly manipulable controls that users can refine rather than committing AI interpretations directly to finished edits. In a within-subjects study with 12 practitioners, participants preferred AI-composed controls, described them as supporting creative exploration, and actively refined AI proposals. However, experiences of control were mixed, and interviews highlighted limited insight into why particular controls and values were proposed. Our findings suggest that making AI interpretations actionable through manipulable controls can support exploration and refinement, but actionability alone does not make those interpretations transparent to all users.

papers.title: Physics with Radioactive Ion Beams at the Nuclear Science Laboratory
papers.summary: The University of Notre Dame is home to a rich history of nuclear science efforts, including some of the earliest developments in the production and creation of radioactive ion beams (RIBs). The resulting TwinSol facility stands as the longest continuously-operating RIB facility in the United States, and has enabled a wide range of experimental efforts in nuclear structure, astrophysics and fundamental symmetries through in-flight RIBs one to two nucleons from stability. A recent upgrade to TwinSol via a third solenoid constituted the founding of the TriSol facility, which provides cleaner, better-focused RIBs to downstream experiments. In this paper, we present a summary of RIB science at the Nuclear Science Laboratory (NSL) with both TwinSol and TriSol and discuss recent upgrades and future experimental plans at the facilities.

papers.title: $^{16}$O(p,$γ$)$^{17}$F Reaction and the C and O Isotopic Ratios in Red Giant Branch Stars
papers.summary: The $^{16}$O/$^{17}$O isotopic ratio is a widely used tracer of nucleosynthesis and mixing processes in red giant stars. Its value depends on the rates of the proton-capture reactions responsible for the production and destruction of $^{16}$O and $^{17}$O among which the $^{16}$O(p,$γ$)$^{17}$F reaction plays a central role, as it involves both isotopes. This work reports on a new measurement of the $^{16}$O(p,$γ$)$^{17}$F cross section carried out at the Laboratory for Underground Nuclear Astrophysics (LUNA) over a center-of-mass energy range of 200 - 380 keV, a region previously unexplored by experimental studies. Two complementary techniques were employed: prompt gamma-ray detection and activation. The results obtained with the two techniques are consistent within experimental uncertainties. From the measured cross sections and existing literature data, we evaluate a new thermonuclear reaction rate, which is then used to demonstrate how simultaneous measurements of stellar carbon and oxygen isotopic ratios constrain the initial mass and the extent of the mixing events in red giant branch stars. In particular, we demonstrate how the $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C abundance ratio is primarily sensitive to the temperature T$_{\textrm{max}}$ attained during mixing, whereas the $^{16}$O/$^{17}$O abundance ratio is highly sensitive to the initial stellar mass M$_i$. Therefore, simultaneous measurements of these isotopic ratios can disentangle and place stringent constraints on M$_i$ and T$_{\textrm{max}}$, and the remaining uncertainty is now dominated by stellar abundance measurements rather than nuclear-physics inputs.

papers.title: Let Me Clarify: Interactive Modeling of Soft Attributes
papers.summary: People commonly express preferences through soft attributes such as is interesting,'' which are difficult to operationalize for computational preference modeling. Latent representations can obscure how such attributes are interpreted, limiting transparency and user control. We formalize softness as the diversity of valid interpretations a description permits and provide empirical support for this characterization. Our proposed measure estimates softness to guide clarification and determine when to generate computational approximations. This is instantiated in AttriFy, a mixed-initiative system that translates descriptions into executable Python functions over text corpora. An interactive dashboard connects the dialogue to proposed functions and computed values, enabling users to inspect, accept, reject, and refine interpretations. An exploratory within-subjects study with 32 participants compares our softness-guided clarification approach with an LLM baseline in supporting interpretable attribute construction. This work positions softness as a basis for constructing explicit, user-steerable attribute dimensions for downstream preference elicitation and decision-making.

papers.title: What and Where in Identifying and Quantifying Conventions in Humans and AI Agents
papers.summary: Cooperative success rests in part on implicit communication. Partners converge on conventions: regularities that give an action meaning beyond its direct effect. Yet conventions are usually observed only indirectly: a score drop when partners are swapped shows that a convention existed, but not what it was or where it was used. In the card game Hanabi, the exact probability that a play fails can be computed from the hints received and the cards in view. Players who use conventions succeed more often than this prediction allows; the resulting margin is the convention gap. Off-belief learning provides a hierarchy of agents (levels 1-5) whose first level uses no conventions by construction and whose later levels use progressively more. For humans and these agents on one scale, we ask what the conventions are and where they are used. On what: in two independently collected corpora of human games, humans show a larger gap than every agent level. On the conventions both populations use, however, humans do no better than level 2. The human advantage is concentrated in a situation that no agent level learns to use: hints that point to a card other than the ones they touch. On where: conventions depend on what the player already knows about the card, not on how recently it was hinted, and they are used most in the mid-game; humans use them earlier and later in the game than the agents. In interventions on the agents, blocking a single high-gap situation costs little, because meaning reroutes to other situations, but blocking several together costs far more than the sum of the single costs. Thus, the convention gap turns conventions from an inferred cause of score loss into a measurable, comparable, and causally testable object.

papers.title: The Body-Algorithm-Emotion Loop: Making Emotion AI Misrecognition Visible through Artistic Practice
papers.summary: This pictorial presents The Body in Algorithmic Colonialism, a screen-based interactive installation that critically examines Emotion-AI through artistic practice. The work uses facial tracking to simulate how commercial Emotion-AI systems translate facial movement into emotional categories and verdicts of compliance or non-compliance. Rather than treating explainability as technical transparency alone, the installation approaches XAI as an embodied encounter with misrecognition: viewers experience how the body is measured, classified, and returned to itself through algorithmic thresholds. Drawing on critical AI studies, affect theory, and practice-as-research, the pictorial positions artistic practice as a method for making affective classification visible and contestable. It documents the conceptual framework, technical process, and critical context of a prototype developed in the first year of a practice-based PhD. No audience responses, interviews, or participant data are analysed in this submission.
papers.comment: In Proceedings of Explainable AI for the Arts Workshop 2026 (XAIxArts 2026) arXiv:2607.20131

papers.title: Auction-based allocation of routes in capacity-constrained networks
papers.summary: We study the route-set allocation problem between end nodes in capacity-constrained flow networks with transfer costs. We introduce an origin--destination (OD) bidding language, in which a participant bids for bounded conic combinations of inlet--outlet--quantity licences and the mechanism performs the routing through a network-flow optimising winner-determination problem. We then study payment rules for the OD mechanism. Under a restricted model with openly and uniformly priced sources and bidders who are indifferent to the source of the gas, the Vickrey--Clarke--Groves (VCG) payment is core-stable; the key structural fact is that in this regime some optimal aggregate flows never use a physical pipe in both directions, so the winner-determination problem reduces to a single-commodity network flow whose value is submodular in the set of active bidders. If source access is allowed to depend on the individual consumer -- a realistic feature, e.g. when gas deals are embedded in bilateral political bargaining -- the reduction fails and VCG payments may lie strictly outside the core. For this general model we propose a dual (nodal) pricing rule derived from the shadow prices of the flow-conservation constraints, and prove it is always core-stable, at the cost of dominant-strategy incentive compatibility. Illustrative examples accompany each result.

papers.title: Task-State Governance: A Virtual Machine for Verifiable and Recoverable GUI Agent Execution
papers.summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents now execute workflows across real applications, but when execution drifts, users must determine what changed, what should have remained untouched, and what can still be recovered. Plan-centric interfaces leave users supervising procedure, but users live with changes to application state. We introduce task-state governance, an interaction paradigm that represents a task as an editable contract linking desired outcomes, facts that must be preserved, and observed application state. We instantiate this paradigm in TaskVM, which projects live state into editable task controls, executes user edits as genuine interface actions, verifies outcomes through independent observation, and marks each action as reversible, compensatable, or irreversible. Across an automated contract benchmark, a controlled user study, and an open live-model exploration, the paradigm strengthened contract compliance and users' recovery control and trust, while execution outcomes were held constant. Task contracts open a design space for governable agent interfaces.

papers.title: Scoping the Landscape of Large Language Model-based Affective Personal Informatics: Review, Reflection, Future Direction
papers.summary: Affective personal informatics (PI) involves capturing, tracking, analyzing, and reflecting on personal data to support emotional self-awareness and mental well-being. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) are reshaping affective PI, yet a comprehensive survey of LLM-based affective PI systems is lacking. To bridge this gap, we systematically analyzed 45 papers published between January 2020 and June 2026 across four major computing and health databases, examining their macro trends, system taxonomies, and research methodologies. Our synthesis reveals an overreliance on multi-stage, text-centric pipelines, a predominance of active, screen-bound interactions, and a severe demographic skew toward young, university-campus-based cohorts in empirical evaluations. Based on these findings, we critically reflect on prevailing architectural and methodological shortcomings and outline actionable future directions for building end-to-end multimodal, low-burden, and inclusive affective PI systems.

papers.title: Feasibility of a Patient-Specific Digital Twin for Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt Trajectory Planning
papers.summary: Catheter obstruction is the commonest cause of shunt failure; freehand insertion at Keen's point leaves the tip free in cerebrospinal fluid in only one case in ten. We built a digital twin that reconstructs skull, scalp, ear and ventricles from preoperative CT by deterministic geometry, searches every entry around Keen's point for the perpendicular trajectory with the longest intraventricular length under safety constraints, and returns the plan as two ruler measurements from the ear and two depths. Executed freehand in 11 consecutive adults (IDEAL Stage 2a), it achieved Hayhurst Grade 1 placement in 10 of 11 against 22 of 213 historically (p = 9 x 10^-9), median entry and angular deviations 2.5 mm and 5.9 degrees, 1.4 cm more intraventricular catheter than Keen's point, and no intraoperative complication. The technique was unchanged; the gain came from choosing entry and depth per patient. Whether it lowers revision is the next stage's hypothesis.
papers.comment: 29 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables; includes Supplementary Information

papers.title: Constraining three-nucleon forces in nuclear lattice effective field theory
papers.summary: We study short-range three-nucleon forces (3NFs) in nuclear lattice effective field theory with a chiral two-nucleon interaction at N${}^3$LO. The one-pion-exchange ($c_D$) and contact ($c_E$) terms of the leading 3NF are decomposed into locally and non-locally smeared components and supplemented by partial-wave-resolved pair contacts coupled to the density of a third nucleon. We determine their coefficients from nuclear binding energies for nuclei in the mass range from $A=3$ to $A=40$ and neutron--alpha finite-volume energies. This allows to work out the minimal three-nucleon force that can be used for future precision studies in NLEFT.

papers.title: Data-Driven Dynamic Portfolio Selection with Vine Copula Simulation and Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: We develop a data-driven approach to dynamic portfolio selection that combines vine-copula simulation with reinforcement learning. The investor has constant relative risk aversion and maximises expected terminal utility with a running penalty on the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of one-period losses. We estimate a conditional vine model from historical returns and use it to generate joint scenarios for CVaR evaluation and conditional paths for training a recurrent portfolio policy. Under uniform local derivative bounds, we propagate edgewise pair-copula parameter errors through the conditional transforms to obtain power-law stability bounds in Hellinger distance and total variation. In a finite-horizon investment model, we combine these estimates with a marginal and structural approximation budget to bound policy values, optimal values and the true-market loss of policies selected under a fitted model, with separate simulation and numerical optimisation terms. On a seven-asset panel comprising US and Chinese equities and gold, the selected ensemble of ten trained policies achieves a compound annual growth rate of 34.13% and a Sharpe ratio of 2.31 over 22 complete monthly holding periods, exceeding the corresponding values of six classical and vine-based benchmarks. Combining simulated and historical training data reduces monthly target-to-target turnover by 41.5% relative to training on historical data alone, while maintaining comparable growth.

papers.title: Interior smoothness and zero-variance geometry for finite-maturity Heston American puts
papers.summary: We study finite-maturity American puts in the Heston model without the Feller condition. At positive variance, the exercise boundary is smooth and strictly decreasing in remaining maturity and variance. At zero variance, the endpoint is locally Lipschitz in remaining maturity, the boundary moves with bounded speed in maturity uniformly down to zero variance, and it extends continuously to the axis. Each boundary slice at positive maturity has a regular $C^1$ closure tangent to the zero-variance axis, its stock threshold has variance derivative tending to minus infinity, and both partial derivatives of the inverse boundary graph vanish along the slice. The continuation premium at the axis contact stock is of order variance, and as a consequence smooth fit fails in the variance direction at the axis. At expiry the whole boundary, including its axis edge, converges to the strike. We give quantitative boundary gap bounds, an exact limiting weighted boundary Hessian, and vertical identities retaining the maturity term. Exact boundary gap equivalents remain open.

papers.title: ShadAR: Real-time Prompting On-demand Visual Augmentation in Augmented Reality
papers.summary: Augmented Reality can reshape our visual perception (e.g., simulating color blindness) yet such effects are typically pre-programmed by experts, making visual augmentation static and inflexible. We introduce ShadAR, an AR system that allows users to describe expected visual augmentations (e.g., "Blur all people") for changing their vision in real time. ShadAR can graphically manipulate AR passthrough in real time via shader injection. When receiving a user's prompt, ShadAR uses LLMs (GPT5.2) to interpret the user's intent, analyzes the user's view with object detection (YOLOv26), generates a pixel shader, and applies it to the targeted region on AR passthrough. To understand usage patterns, we invited 21 HCI researchers to use ShadAR, identifying four application domains (design, health, productivity, and social interaction) and two prompt-framing patterns: procedural prompts specifying what to modify and how ("Highlight the book."), and end-goal prompts conveying desired mental or behavioral states ("Make me laugh."). Such end-goal prompts suggest a future in which users specify outcomes (e.g., "Make me not miss my flight") while the system determines how to realize them, though often with inherently indeterminate results. We discuss design opportunities for ShadAR and ethical concerns.

papers.title: Think Once, Reflect Twice: How Feedback Shapes Human-AI Collaboration
papers.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports human decision-making in high-stakes domains, designing effective human-AI collaboration becomes critical. Successful collaboration requires humans to reflect on decision-making processes and adjust their strategies accordingly. Current research typically investigates interventions, such as explainable AI, that target reflection during the decision-making process (reflection-in-action). Less attention has been given to retrospective examination of decisions (reflection-on-action). This work explores reflection-on-action by studying the impact of feedback on reliance behavior and human-AI team performance. Specifically, we investigate feedback interventions targeting overrides of AI advice through a behavioral study (N=244). We find that such feedback influences reflection-on-action, while unidirectional feedback risks reducing subsequent reflection-in-action. Furthermore, we identify opposing shifts in reliance behavior that leave overall human-AI team performance unchanged but show context-dependent effects. Balanced feedback did not show these risks, preserving both concurrent and retrospective reflection, offering insights for designing for appropriate reliance on AI.

papers.title: EEG Correlates of Verbal and Perceptual Reasoning
papers.summary: Identifying the neural underpinnings of intelligence is one of the major goals of modern intelligence research. However, few imaging studies explore the high extremes of intelligence, and most use only a single composite IQ score. This study used quantitative EEG recordings to investigate correlations between the EEG variables of individual alpha peak frequency, relative power, and coherence, and scores on verbal and perceptual reasoning tests in participants with IQs from the low-average to exceptionally gifted ranges. Overall, the results did not reveal any pattern of significant relationships between these EEG measures and the two psychometric tests. Since this study had only a small sample, heavily skewed towards the high-IQ end of the scale, no definitive conclusions about the EEG measures and verbal and perceptual reasoning can be drawn. Nevertheless, it reveals many opportunities for further research, and suggestions are made for progressing this topic in the future.

papers.title: AdaptaFace: Adversarial Assistance for Inclusive Facial Gesture Interaction
papers.summary: Facial gestures can enable access for people with motor impairments (PwM), yet recognizers may not reliably interpret individual facial movement patterns. Existing approaches either constrain agency by requiring predefined templates or impose repeated calibration, data collection, and computation through user-specific retraining. We present AdaptaFace, an input-level compatibility layer using bounded, proxy-dependent adversarial perturbations to translate user-compatible gestures into inputs for an unchanged facial action unit (AU)-based recognizer. Designed around six personalization principles informed by interviews with 12 PwM, AdaptaFace supports both recognition enhancement and gesture vocabulary extension. In a within-subject study with 16 participants, AdaptaFace increased task completion from 59.7% to 90.5% and reduced workload from 5.61 to 4.21. Offline validation showed strong steering with aligned perturbation generation and evaluation but weaker cross-recognizer transfer, defining the approach's boundary. These findings frame adversarial assistance as input-side accessibility mediation for personalized facial-gesture interaction.

papers.title: Reciprocity coordinates a three-way trade-off in recurrent neural circuits
papers.summary: Biological neural circuits contain both unidirectional and reciprocal connections, but how reciprocity affects circuit computation remains unclear. We varied reciprocity \r{ho} across 21 levels in recurrent-network simulations while holding network size, connection density, and directed-edge count fixed. Low-reciprocity networks produced more diverse stimulus-driven activity and performed better on four continuous-input tasks, whereas higher reciprocity generally improved performance on three delayed-memory tasks. Increasing reciprocity reduced online memory capacity and accelerated recovery from perturbations. A post-cue noise experiment showed that higher reciprocity suppressed internal noise propagation but made cue-evoked states less distinguishable, and component matching separated the contributions of cue separation and within-cue dispersion to readout robustness. Within this ensemble, reciprocity thus mediates a three-way trade-off among representational capacity, local stability, and task-state separability: higher reciprocity lowers capacity, strengthens stability, and compresses separability. Whether it improves behaviour depends on whether the stability gain outweighs the lost separation between task states. Connectome and microcircuit datasets from five species showed intermediate reciprocity, while reciprocity varied substantially across adult Drosophila brain regions, providing compatible structural context and motivating circuit-specific functional tests.

papers.title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters
papers.summary: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.

papers.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
papers.summary: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

papers.title: Which Text Matters: Handling Model Uncertainty in Text-as-Data Regressions, with an Application to Central Bank Communication
papers.summary: Social scientists routinely convert text into covariates like topic shares, ideal points or sentiment scores, and insert them into statistical models of interest. This two-step design is convenient, but it is rarely guided by theory: little tells the analyst which text-based covariates to construct or include. Each approach embodies contestable measurement choices, and competing operationalizations of the same construct can support different conclusions, so a single research question gives rise to a menu of competing regression models. Which text constructed covariates belong in a model, and in what functional form, is thus a problem of model uncertainty. We propose spike-and-slab generalized additive models (SSGAMs), which jointly select covariates and determine whether their effects are linear or nonlinear. We illustrate the approach with the communication of a powerful unelected institution, asking which of 45 competing text indicators from 224 monthly European Central Bank press conferences, spanning late 2002 to mid-2025, track professional inflation expectations. A sparse set is selected; widely used alternatives, and every tested nonlinear effect, carry no incremental information.

papers.title: Probing the production mechanisms of virtual photons at RHIC
papers.summary: We report the measurement of direct virtual photon ($γ^*_\text{dir} \rightarrow e^+e^-$) in four Au+Au collision energies at $\sqrt{s_\text{NN}}$ = 14.6--54.4 GeV. The $γ^*_\text{dir}$ yields scale with charged-particle multiplicity ($(dN_{\mathrm{ch}}/dη)^α$) as $α=1.43 \pm 0.04 \text{(stat.)} \pm 0.03\text{(sys.)}$, independent of collision energies and centralities, exceeding hadronic expectations and indicating notable contribution from QGP phase. At $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=$ 54.4 GeV, the direct virtual photon mass distributions are further studied over $0.1 < M_{ee} < 1.1$ GeV/$c^2$, and are found to evolve from exponential to power-law form with increasing $p_\text{T}$, signaling a shift from "blackbody" radiation to emission governed by Kroll-Wada formalism.

papers.title: Collective-flow signatures of bubble nuclei in intermediate-energy projectile fragmentation reactions
papers.summary: Characterized by central density depletion, bubble nuclei represent an important class of exotic nuclear structures. Collective flow in the $^{40}$Ca+$^{9}$Be projectile fragmentation reaction at 140 MeV/u is investigated using the extended quantum molecular dynamics (EQMD) model with a parameter on of the isoscalar monopole excitation strength $\varepsilon$. The projectile $^{40}Ca$ is initialized as a relaxed ten-$α$ cluster configuration exhibiting a bubble-like density distribution. The results reveal that increasing $\varepsilon$ modifies the density distribution and the size of the depleted central region of bubble, producing pronounced changes in fragment yields and collective flow around $\varepsilon\approx0.5$. Below this value, heavy-fragment production plays a significant role, while the directed flow $v_1$ of protons and neutrons remains predominantly negative, indicating preferential emission toward the target side. Above $\varepsilon\approx0.5$, enhanced expansion of the central low-density region suppresses heavy residues and drives $v_1$ toward positive values. In contrast, preformed $α$ clusters show different responses, reflecting their origin in the initial cluster configuration rather than solely in secondary decay. At low excitation, the cluster flow exhibits a pronounced impact-parameter dependence, whereas stronger excitation weakens cluster binding and suppresses directional anisotropy, driving the flow close to zero. The rapidity slopes of the flow coefficients also vary systematically with $\varepsilon$, tracing changes in emission anisotropy during expansion. These findings extend traditional static descriptions by probing the dynamical evolution of exotic structures in heavy-ion reactions and the contrasting collective-flow behavior of preformed clusters and single nucleons constitutes a sensitive dynamical probe of bubble-like structures.

papers.title: R-process nuclei in the rare-earth region above N=126 in Relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory: A preponderance of shape-coexistence in nuclei
papers.summary: The shell structure of nuclei beyond N=126 relevant to the third peak at A ~ 195 in r-process nuclear abundances in investigated. Within the framework of the relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in deformed space, a comparative study of the response of nuclei with three different model Lagrangians NL-SV1, SVI-2 and NL3 is made. Ground-state properties of even-even nuclei in the isotopic chains of Z=58-72$= in the highly neutron-rich region are investigated. A comparison of binding energies with mass formulas shows that in the extreme region of the r-process path, the RMF model SVI-2 without nonlinearities of sigma and omega mesons shows an excellent agreement with the mass formula HFB-24. It is shown that in all the above Lagrangian models, in the neutron rich region between the shell closures N=126 and N=184, there is a preponderance of nuclides exhibiting coexistence of well-deformed prolate and oblate shapes in the ground state. A prolate ground state is shown to evolve smoothly to a coexisting oblate ground state via a near degeneracy with successive addition of neutrons. Induced by an onset of deformation for $N \ge 130$, nuclei approaching the r-process path are shown to exhibit enhanced stability in many isotopic chains (Z > 60). This has the effect of shifting the expected neutron drip line significantly farther into the neutron-rich region especially for the higher Z chains. Consequences of the enhanced stability, the shape co-existence and degeneracy of shapes in nuclei on the r-process nucleosynthesis are discussed.

papers.title: Building a Sovereign Benchmark The Limits of Private Coordination
papers.summary: Public debt supplies liquidity and collateral services only if institutions coordinate on using the same claim. We study this coordination when use carries a recurring cost and a benefit that rises with other users. Above a quality threshold, two positive-adoption equilibria exist, and under best responses the initial user base decides between collapse and high adoption. Under logit choice, as the population grows and noise vanishes, the long-run distribution selects high adoption only above a strictly higher threshold. Debt issuance improves market depth but eventually dilutes backing per claim. This trade-off creates a range of debt levels supporting the liquidity premium of public debt in macroeconomic models and a narrower range supporting its long-run selection. At the boundary of the wider range, the premium is discontinuous. A matching transfer that corrects the adoption externality makes stationary selection maximize network surplus. Transfers can also help launch a network without permanent support.

papers.title: Rewarding Noise: Incentives in Decentralized A/B Testing
papers.summary: Many firms that run A/B tests struggle with low statistical power, increasing the risk that launch decisions are driven by noise rather than true impact. We argue that in decentralized organizations, low power can reflect misaligned incentives: product teams choose what and how to test on a customer-facing experience to maximize their private reward, while the experience owner sets evaluation rules and launch criteria to optimize the experience. We formalize this interaction via a principal-agent model and show that evaluating tests using raw impact estimates creates a reward to sampling noise. Correctly calibrated posterior-mean evaluation removes this reward and creates a local incentive to reallocate toward fewer, more precise tests of more ambitious ideas. Using data on A/B tests run at Amazon, we document patterns consistent with these model predictions. After an Amazon experience shifted to posterior-mean-based evaluation in 2024, test volume declined while both precision and the dispersion of true impacts increased, more than doubling signal-to-noise ratios. Our results highlight that A/B testing methodologies can shape not only measurement and launch decisions, but which tests are pursued in the first place.

papers.title: Structure Before Intelligence: Gating What Agentic Scientific Workflows Release
papers.summary: An agentic scientific workflow can run to completion and still release wrong results: a silent numerical error, a stale input, or a defect in a shared upstream step can contaminate several outputs while a sibling branch stays correct. We treat trust in such results as a release decision. A harness around the workflow's directed acyclic graph (DAG) decides which outputs may be used: it enforces mandatory checks, contains failures to the affected branch, recomputes from tracked versions, adds validators, and releases a result only if a risk model estimates its probability of being invalid as low. Language-model agents work inside the harness, choosing corrective actions and reviewing releases, but cannot override it. On 60 held-out paired instances of two workflows with injected faults, we switched components on and off. Each supplied a different property. Containment and recovery raised the number of correct results. Validation supplied safety: fixed rules without validation released 37 invalid results, while validating every candidate released none. Risk estimation supplied efficiency, matching that safety with 31% fewer validators at somewhat lower yield, although better targeting than random validation was not shown. Lineage evidence helped on one workflow. The language model added no measurable benefit: whether invalid results escaped depended on the harness, not the model. This proof of concept points to a practical path: placing agents inside explicit release-control structure can keep released scientific results trustworthy, and it gives more capable agents a measurable baseline to improve on.
papers.comment: 21 pages: 10-page main paper and 11-page supplement; 2 figures

papers.title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
papers.summary: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.

papers.title: Binding energies in the $0^{-+}$ and $1^{--}$ fermion--antifermion channels from the ladder Bethe-Salpeter and Schrödinger equations
papers.summary: In this work, we calculate the binding energies of an equal-mass fermion--antifermion system in the $0^{-+}$ and $1^{--}$ channels from the ladder Bethe--Salpeter (BS) equation with scalar, pseudoscalar, and vector exchange. The results are compared with those of the Schrödinger equation with the corresponding leading static interaction in two regimes: pointlike massless exchange at weak coupling and finite-mass exchange with monopole form factors at stronger coupling. For the BS calculation, we use two independent numerical methods based on momentum-space integral equations and coordinate-space differential equations. The differential-equation method gives estimated relative binding-energy errors below $10^{-9}$ in both regimes. For massless vector exchange in Coulomb gauge, the numerical results are consistent with the uncrossed-ladder perturbative spectrum through the $O(mα^5)$ terms. The results for massless scalar exchange and vector exchange in Feynman gauge are consistent with the common Wick--Cutkosky expansion through order $mα^3$. For finite exchange masses, the differences from the leading static Schrödinger spectra at the same masses, couplings, and form factors depend strongly on the exchange and channel. Scalar exchange gives nearly degenerate channels with much weaker binding than the Schrödinger reference. In contrast, vector exchange with only the metric term retained gives stronger binding than the Schrödinger reference in $0^{-+}$ and weaker binding in $1^{--}$. Notably, retaining the full Proca numerator substantially increases the vector binding in both channels. Pseudoscalar exchange also supports bound states and favors $1^{--}$, although its leading static central interaction vanishes.

papers.title: Constraints on pion parton distributions at small $x$ from leading-neutron electroproduction data
papers.summary: We revisit the extraction of parton distribution functions (PDFs) in the pion in a global QCD analysis of pion--nucleus Drell--Yan and leading-neutron (LN) electroproduction data, in view of recent suggestions that uncertainties on the pion PDFs at small parton momentum fraction $x$ are dramatically underestimated. We perform a set of controlled fits that vary the LN data coverage, PDF parametrization, and positivity constraints, determining both the PDFs and pion-nucleon splitting functions simultaneously. While the use of a restricted H1 LN data sample used by the Fantômas group is found to enlarge the PDF uncertainties and admit solutions with vanishing gluon PDFs, our global analysis provides a good description of an extended H1 and ZEUS LN database, significantly reducing the parametrization dependence and strongly disfavoring a zero gluon distribution.

papers.title: Strange-quark-number-dependent response to partonic dynamics in baryon-rich Au+Au collisions
papers.summary: We identify a strange-quark-number-dependent hierarchy in the response to explicit partonic dynamics by comparing PHSD5.2 with its hadron--string limit in baryon-rich Au+Au collisions at $\snn=3.0$--$7.2$~GeV. Crossing the local conversion threshold alone does not ensure a visible final-state signal: abundant-hadron flow changes little at 3--4.5~GeV, whereas the fractional yield response becomes ordered at 6.2--7.2~GeV, reaching $S_{|s|=1}\simeq0.2$--$0.3$, $S_{|s|=2}\simeq0.65$, and $S_{|s|=3}\simeq0.93$ at 7.2~GeV. The hierarchy is consistent with an enlarged recombination phase space for strange constituents released from different pre-hadronic sources, but does not by itself establish an increase in the total $s+\bar s$ abundance or stronger strange-quark clustering. Since $S_X$ is a model-defined response rather than a direct observable, matched excitation functions of $Ξ^-/Λ$ and $Ω^-/Λ$, together with high-$m_T$ proton elliptic flow, provide experimentally accessible discriminants between the predicted PHSD and HSD dynamics.

papers.title: Effects of cortisol time-scales in a model of emotion regulation
papers.summary: Stress reshapes cortico-limbic dynamics across multiple timescales, with important consequences for healthy and pathological arousal responses. We develop and analyze a Wilson-Cowan model of prefrontal-amygdala circuitry, incorporating excitatory and inhibitory populations involved in emotional regulation. The effects of stress cortisol are represented as history-dependent modulations of two stress-sensitive interactions: recurrent prefrontal excitation and inhibition of basolateral amygdala principal cells. Using numerical simulations and bifurcation analysis, we examine how this self-interacting system organizes transitions between stable activity and infra-slow oscillations, and how this structure changes with cortisol-related temporal memory. To distinguish the effects of memory temporal distribution from those of its timescale, we compare weak and strong Gamma kernels with a discrete-delay limit, representing progressively different ways in which past activity can influence current coupling. Introducing temporal memory reshapes the parameter region supporting oscillations and alters their persistence. Weak and strong Gamma kernels produce remarkably similar global dynamics, whereas the discrete-delay limit generates a substantially richer bifurcation structure, including quasiperiodic activity. Together, these results suggest that the dynamical effects of cortisol depend not only on the characteristic timescale of its action, but also on the shape of the temporal memory through which past neural activity influences the present. Different forms of temporal integration may provide a mechanism by which neural systems implement distinct functional dynamics, while changes in this integration could promote atypical or pathological rhythmic regimes.

papers.title: An Open-Source Web-Based Viewer for Disseminating Image-Derived Models
papers.summary: Patient-specific 3-dimensional (3D) models are increasingly central to planning surgery and catheter-based intervention in children with congenital heart disease (CHD), whose anatomy is often atypical and variable. These models inform care only when the surgeons and interventional cardiologists who make treatment decisions can rotate, crop, and measure them directly. Desktop modeling applications require local installation, capable hardware, and training. Commercial web-based viewers are portable but closed, and, in our experience, cannot display volume rendering, time-resolved (e.g., 4-dimensional) data, or the custom workflows centers build for CHD. Because CHD populations are small and heterogeneous, such workflows are unlikely to be prioritized commercially, and end users have no means to add them. To address these limitations, we developed the SlicerHeart Viewer, an open-source module that presents a simplified interface to a complete 3D Slicer/SlicerHeart session running on a server. Clinicians access models created by clinical modeling services from any device through a web browser. Because 3D Slicer runs underneath, volume rendering, time-resolved data, and any SlicerHeart workflow, including those developed for CHD, are available without modification. The module is independent of the hosting environment; we chose internal servers behind institutional single sign-on, and a cloud-hosted option is in development. Over one year at a single pediatric center, nearly all of 82 modeled cases were shared through the Viewer with clinicians from five specialties, with cases loading in 5 to 10 seconds. The approach is not specific to CHD and is deployable at other centers.

papers.title: Simulating Alzheimer's amyloid-like pathology on a fly central nervous system connectome
papers.summary: In Alzheimer's disease, the amount of pathology in the brain is an imperfect predictor of how much function is lost. Pathology leads to that loss through neural circuits, but these cannot be observed neuron by neuron in patients. This study therefore simulated the central nervous system of the adult male Drosophila melanogaster: 166,700 integrate-and-fire neurons wired by the MaleCNS connectome. The simulator reproduced a published fly brain model (rate correlation 0.9997). Three kinds of damage reported in amyloid-$β$ flies, a lowered spike threshold, synapse loss and neuron loss, were imposed with assumed magnitudes, and circuit responses were measured in 1,424 simulated flies. The number of neurons lost was a poor guide to the deficit, which depended partly on how many synaptic contacts went with them and whether they included input neurons or one command neuron. With the same 12% of neurons removed, odour-evoked whole-brain activity was 93%, 47% or 31% of the healthy value when damage fell on poorly connected, random or highly connected neurons; these flies lost 20%, 35% and 48% of contacts. When the contacts lost were equalised, the three groups differed less; whether the remaining difference reflects where the damage fell could not be established. In 48 flies, restoring only the contacts that surviving neurons had lost recovered 62% of the whole-brain deficit, and restoring the removed neurons 39%. In flies that had lost neurons delivering the odour, these accounted for about half the deficit due to neuron loss. One neuron could decide an outcome: all 66 flies that lost the giant fibre on the stimulated side, which commands escape, had a giant fibre rate below 100 Hz, against 1 of 254 that kept it. Whole-brain activity revealed damage at milder severity than the learning index, because it changed much relative to its variation between trials.
papers.comment: 104 pages: main text 51 pages with 7 figures and 4 supporting figures, followed by S1 Text (53 pages). Code and per-fly result tables: https://github.com/taehojo/adfly-connectome

papers.title: Deep Generative Models for Phylogenetic Inference with Complex Evolutionary Processes
papers.summary: Inference of phylogenetic trees from sequences plays a central role in understanding evolutionary relationships, with applications ranging from tracking pathogen spread to reconstructing the history of life. Conventionally, practitioners obtain posteriors over trees using likelihood-based methods like MCMC. However, likelihoods are only available for simple evolutionary models with restrictive assumptions. For realistic evolutionary models, inference using conventional methods is prohibitively expensive, inaccurate, or even impossible. In practice, practitioners settle for using as flexible a conventional method as possible, even though they expect it is misspecified. In principle, we could use simulation-based inference: simulate tree and sequence data from an evolutionary model and train a neural network to predict the posterior over trees given sequences. However it is a mathematical challenge to represent and train complex posterior distributions over trees. Here we present a flexible family of conditional generative models over trees. Our models iteratively build trees using three natural paradigms -- top-down, middle-out, or bottom-up -- and are trained using a discrete diffusion framework. For real and synthetic datasets of up to $65$ taxa and $>10^5$ tokens, our models recover MCMC posteriors much more accurately than the previous state-of-the-art simulation-based method Phyloformer 2. Finally, we compare to IQ-Tree, a popular flexible-but-misspecified conventional method. Our models match its tree estimates on simple data, but on more realistic data, our method is reliably more accurate.
papers.journal: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

papers.title: Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
papers.summary: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.

papers.title: A 4D $T^\prime$-expanded lattice QCD equation of state with a multi-dimensional 3D-Ising-type critical contribution
papers.summary: Inferring the possible existence and location of a critical point on the QCD phase diagram through experimental observations requires equations of state that include both lattice QCD constraints and critical behavior. In this manuscript, we present the first four-dimensional equation of state in the $(T,μ_B,μ_Q,μ_S)$ space combining the lattice 4D $T^\prime$-Expansion Scheme with a critical contribution mapped from the 3D Ising model. We extend the earlier two-dimensional construction, the so-called Ising 2D-TExS in the $(T, μ_B)$ plane, promoting the critical point to a parametrizable critical surface in the full four-dimensional thermodynamic space. Our framework provides a family of equations of state to systematically study the effects of criticality in realistic hydrodynamic simulations with $BQS$ conserved charges, going beyond the case of strangeness neutrality, by varying the geometry of the critical surface and the strength of criticality at finite $μ_B$, $μ_Q$ and $μ_S$ separately.

papers.title: Virtual photon bremsstrahlung in a magnetized quark-gluon-plasma
papers.summary: We investigate dilepton production via virtual quark bremsstrahlung in a hot, magnetized quark-gluon plasma (QGP), extending the Landau-Pomeranchuk-Migdal (LPM) framework to account for a background magnetic field and for Fermi-Dirac quark statistics. An external electromagnetic field drives the quark distribution out of equilibrium, and this off-equilibrium correction, obtained from the Boltzmann equation in the relaxation-time approximation, is in principle explicit in the electric and magnetic field strengths. We argue that this correction, being linear in the electric field, vanishes identically upon integration over the full dilepton solid angle and therefore does not contribute to the dilepton production rate (DPR). The leading magnetic-field signature in the rate instead enters entirely through the equilibrium sector: the medium density and Debye screening mass, computed from the Landau-level structure of the magnetized QGP, modifying the LPM suppression parameter. Working in the regime relevant to the hydrodynamic phase of heavy-ion collisions, we present the LPM-induced DPR for quark scatterers and establish, for the first time, a nonzero magnetic-field imprint on this observable through the LPM mechanism.

papers.title: Shear viscosity from fluctuations in linearized relativistic hydrodynamics
papers.summary: In this work we incorporate thermal fluctuations into fluid-dynamic simulations with the vHLLE code, in linear approximation. The fluctuations are built in following the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. The effect of space discretization into cells in numerical hydrodynamics on the spatial correlation of fluctuations is studied with the help of static structure factor. A difference from the continuum result is pointed out and systematically investigated. Time evolution of the ensuing fluctuations is examined and the Green-Kubo formula is used for the extraction of shear viscosity from the fluctuations. The extracted value is demonstrated to be the same as the input value of the shear viscosity for the simulations using Israel-Stewart equations. It is also shown that numerical regulators commonly used in the codes to ensure stability of the calculation severely spoil the fluctuations and break the fluctuation-dissipation theorem.

papers.title: Femtoscopic parameters of pion emission sources in EPOS4 Au+Au collisions from 7.7 to 200 GeV
papers.summary: Three-dimensional femtoscopy probes the space-time structure of particle-emitting sources in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The collision-energy dependence of Lévy source parameters may reveal the evolution of strongly interacting matter and possible signatures of the QCD phase diagram. We previously studied the excitation function of three-dimensional Lévy source parameters for pion pairs in Au+Au collisions with EPOS4, analyzing the pair-distance distribution \(D(ρ)\) through one-dimensional projections. Here, we analyze the full three-dimensional source distribution and correlation function directly. We construct \(D(ρ_{\rm out},ρ_{\rm side},ρ_{\rm long})\) as a 3D histogram, transform it into \(C(q_{\rm out},q_{\rm side},q_{\rm long})\) using a Fast Fourier Transform, and fit the correlation function with the analytic Lévy formula. This approach can reduce biases arising when one-dimensional projections are used to describe a non-elliptical source. We apply the method across the RHIC Beam Energy Scan range and compare the extracted energy dependence with results from the projection-based method and recent UrQMD calculations. We focus on the out-side observables \(R_{\rm diff}^{2}=R_{\rm out}^{2}-R_{\rm side}^{2}\) and \(R_{\rm out}/R_{\rm side}\), whose different energy dependences in EPOS4 and UrQMD may illuminate the roles of emission duration and source dynamics. This work establishes a direct three-dimensional framework for comparison with future femtoscopic measurements and for exploring possible non-monotonic structures associated with the QCD phase diagram.
